slides.title: Build a multimodal pipeline with nirs4all
presenter_action: Start with one source.
Add another measurement.
Choose where to combine them.
slides.speaker_notes: Open with the concrete task: predict one target using several measurements of the same observations. We will build and edit three real pipelines, rather than tour a menu of fusion names. In the editor, S1/S2/S3 identify source inputs; B1/B2 identify model branches. Early fusion connects several sources to one model branch, not to several predictors. Explain the session: 21 minutes of support, 17 minutes of live editing and 2 minutes of discussion.
slides.takeaway: One editable pipeline, several ways to combine its sources.

slides.title: One observation, three complementary views
presenter_action: Raman + NIRS + MIR: three spectra.
NIRS + markers: different information.
NIRS + image: spectrum and spatial pattern.
slides.speaker_notes: Show actual sample-002 in the supplied synthetic examples. Raman has 48 variables, NIRS 64 and MIR 56; genetics has 16 dosage markers; images are 12 by 12 grayscale. One observation ID links the views. Ask what the second source might add to prediction. Keep the answer open; there is no promise that more sources improve a model.
slides.takeaway: A second source can add information, redundancy or noise.

slides.title: Early, intermediate and late: what enters the merge?
presenter_action: Source → source-specific steps.
Merge variables, features or predictions.
A predictor produces the common target.
slides.speaker_notes: Read the three comparison rows. Early combines variables before a common predictor; intermediate combines learned features before a common head; late combines outputs after separate source models. Give the numerical examples visible in the table:168 spectral variables,6 + 6 learned features and 3 source predictions. These are editable explanatory diagrams, not screenshots or fabricated model outputs.
slides.takeaway: Early combines variables; mid combines learned features; late combines predictions.

slides.title: Start from a one-source pipeline
presenter_action: Keep Raman as the only source.
Inspect its preprocessing and PLS node.
Run and keep this as the reference.
slides.speaker_notes: In the real editor, trace one complete executable path. Point to the source, its actual step parameters and PLS component count. Save the run under an explicit name. This provides the reference to which the next edited pipeline will be compared. Use the actual delivered labels; do not substitute the existing read-only DAG viewer for this editing demonstration.
slides.takeaway: Start with a pipeline you can explain from beginning to end.

slides.title: Early fusion: add the other source inputs
presenter_action: Connect NIRS and MIR to B1.
Keep a separate processing chain per source.
Fit one PLS on the joined columns.
slides.speaker_notes: Build the second pipeline from the baseline by connecting NIRS and MIR as additional source inputs to the existing model B1. New branch would create another predictor, which is not this early-fusion edit. The supplied widths are 48 + 64 + 56 = 168 columns before any width-changing operator. Each source input retains its axis and source identity even though the final learner receives one numerical matrix. Show source inputs S1/S2/S3 feeding the one common predictor B1. Their variables combine inside this joint source operator. Merge kind remains No merge because B1 is the only model branch. The editor provides explicit connections and Merge kind controls; no free dragging of the fusion point is claimed. Ask the audience what changed relative to the baseline before executing.
slides.takeaway: 48 + 64 + 56 = 168 variables; one PLS predicts the common target.

slides.title: Edit one source input or model setting
presenter_action: Disconnect MIR from the early branch.
Select the PLS or NIRS processing node.
Change one setting, then run that draft.
slides.speaker_notes: Disconnect MIR from the early branch and inspect the two remaining source inputs. Run that one structural change before making another. Then restore the full original draft before changing the PLS Components setting from 3 to 6. Separately inspect the NIRS processing node, where a supported transform can be added or reordered. Keep edits separate in the named history so one effect can be interpreted. Slide 17 compares the exact full-source versus disconnected-MIR drafts actually executed.
slides.takeaway: Different sources can have different processing chains.

slides.title: Live 1 · build and edit a spectral pipeline
presenter_action: Open Early fusion and run the starting draft.
Disconnect MIR; edit a selected node.
Run edited pipeline, then Restore a saved run.
slides.speaker_notes: Switch to the actual editor for six minutes. Follow the short runbook in the instructor guide. Use the actual three-pane editor: presets/palette, a model canvas with source inputs, and context inspector. Disconnect a source input from B1 and use Run edited pipeline. Restore the original three-source draft before setting Components to 6 and running it. Source-step edits use the selected source or transform inspector. Do not use New branch to add a measurement; it adds another model. Restore a completed history entry to recover its exact draft. Retain actual recipe/run evidence for before and after. Use recorded runs only if explicitly labelled as such.
slides.takeaway: Demonstration: an edit changes the pipeline that really executes.

slides.title: Late fusion: put a model in each branch
presenter_action: Fit Raman, NIRS and MIR models separately.
Merge their predictions on the target scale.
Use a fixed mean as the first combiner.
slides.speaker_notes: Move conceptually from one shared PLS after the feature merge to one model branch per source followed by a fixed mean. B1/B2/B3 are now three predictors. Use Merge kind to choose Fixed mean of predictions. In the editor, show the actual branch heads and prediction merge, then change one branch head from PLS to Ridge while leaving the other branches and fixed mean explicit. The mean receives three source predictions rather than 168 raw variables. The mean has fixed equal weights; it is not a trained stack. Read the actual native result rather than averaging displayed RMSE values.
slides.takeaway: Three source models produce three aligned predictions; the native mean combines them.

slides.title: Stacking: replace the fixed mean with a learner
presenter_action: Keep several base models.
Use their OOF predictions as new columns.
Fit a Ridge combiner.
slides.speaker_notes: Show PLS/Ridge base heads and the meta-learner in the actual pipeline. The practical change is the input to Ridge: prediction columns. Explain OOF in one sentence: a base prediction used to train the combiner must come from a model that did not fit that row or its group. The visible six-column matrix is the calibration-refit example; outer-fold fits use their own training rows. Native DAG execution provides that procedure. This is enough context for the editing task; do not turn it into several validation slides.
slides.takeaway: Three sources × two base models = six OOF prediction columns for Ridge.

slides.title: Keep blocks visible with multiblock PLS
presenter_action: Keep the same source inputs.
Choose the actual MB-PLS head.
State its block scaling and algorithm.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the concrete early-fusion draft as the comparison. This native MB-PLS head preserves block widths and uses centered blocks with equal super weights. Explain why a chemometrician may want the block identity. It is one named algorithm profile, not every MBPLS variant. Do not claim it must beat concatenated PLS. Keep any detailed scaling formula in the guide, not on this practical slide.
slides.takeaway: The MB-PLS head retains the 48 / 64 / 56 block structure.

slides.title: Live 2 · combine NIRS and genetic markers
presenter_action: Load the paired sources and a late preset.
Change the genetic branch from PLS to Ridge.
Run and restore the starting draft.
slides.speaker_notes: Switch to the real editor for five minutes. Follow NIRS and the 16 genetic-dosage columns for the same sample IDs. Use a dense/tabular interpretation for the markers. Load a late draft, change only the genetic branch head from PLS to Ridge and run it. Use the history to restore the exact starting draft. Show the early or learned-combiner route only as a short comparison if time remains. Mention biological groups at the point where the grouping is visible, without adding a protocol lecture.
slides.takeaway: Different representations share the target, not necessarily the same preprocessing.

slides.title: Intermediate fusion: image and NIRS branches
presenter_action: NIRS 64 → conv1d → embedding 6.
Image 12 × 12 × 1 → conv2d → embedding 6.
Concatenate 12 features → head 8 → target.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the actual image teaching architecture. NIRS has 64 input variables; a conv1d branch learns an embedding of size 6. The 12 × 12 × 1 image enters a conv2d branch and another size 6 embedding. Concatenation gives 12 features, followed by 8 hidden head units and one target. Both source encoders and the head learn together inside one joint model branch B1. The conv1d/conv2d encoders are internal network components, not separate editor model branches B1 and B2. This is an editable architecture explanation, not an invented activation trace or measurement. Network capacity does not guarantee better prediction.
slides.takeaway: Two learned embeddings of size 6 become 12 features for the shared head.

slides.title: Image + NIRS: change the representation, keep the task
presenter_action: Early baseline: flattened pixels + spectrum.
Mid pipeline: image geometry + spectral branch.
Inspect the actual image linked to the same ID.
slides.speaker_notes: Show the real selected 12 by 12 grayscale image and its spectrum. Compare two executable routes: flattened 144 pixel columns joined with 64 spectral columns for PLS; or a conv2d image branch plus a conv1d spectrum branch feeding a learned head. Flattening still retains pixel values, but the learner has no explicit convolutional neighbourhood structure.
slides.takeaway: The same measurements can enter different model representations.

slides.title: Live 3 · edit the image–spectrum pipeline
presenter_action: Open the flattened early baseline, then Mid.
Inspect image conv2d and spectral conv1d.
Edit Embedding size and run the pipeline.
slides.speaker_notes: Switch to the real editor for six minutes. Follow the image and spectral source routes, then change Embedding size in the joint B1 network inspector using the delivered controls. The internal encoders do not appear as independent document model branches. The host derives conv2d/conv1d structure from the actual source shapes; do not suggest editing low-level branch arrays. Inspect the graph/recipe change before fitting. Compare actual current results, including any underperformance; do not tune using the held-out result during the demonstration.
slides.takeaway: Demonstration: source shape, branch kind and learned feature merge are explicit.

slides.title: Hybrid: a source block plus model predictions
presenter_action: Keep a selected transformed source block.
Add legitimate OOF prediction features.
Join them before the final Ridge.
slides.speaker_notes: Trace one concrete hybrid route in the editor. Distinguish the data-source input from the prediction-source input before the join. Explain why the combiner sees both rather than calling every join early fusion. The native hybrid execution aligns the rows and fits the relevant transforms in its current training scope. Keep the exact supported hybrid topology honest; do not promise arbitrary graph compositions the editor cannot execute.
slides.takeaway: A merge can combine different kinds of information if its inputs are explicit.

slides.title: From your edit to the native run
presenter_action: Edit a source, step or model in the UI.
Save its explicit pipeline declaration.
Run source transforms → models → merge.
slides.speaker_notes: Show three large editable panels: actual UI Components = 6, the exact sourceIds and head.params.n_components = 6 fields from the saved declaration, and the native OOF result for 96 observations (RMSE 0.0816857 a.u.). The UI edit becomes an explicit pipeline document, then native execution applies the declared source transforms, model heads and merge. IO has already aligned the source observations. Connect one visible edited field to the actual exported document or generated native recipe; show only a short real excerpt when useful. Restore recovers a saved editable draft; exporting and importing nirs4all.multimodal-pipeline.v1 lets the same accepted declaration be rerun. No invented Python example or implementation-layer catalogue is needed.
slides.takeaway: Your edited sources, steps and merge define the pipeline that really runs.

slides.title: Source selection also changes the capacity needed
presenter_action: Compare all sources with PLS 3.
Disconnect MIR, keeping PLS 3.
Restore all sources and use PLS 6.
slides.speaker_notes: Read three actual native-history rows: all Raman/NIRS/MIR with PLS 3; MIR disconnected with PLS 3; then all sources restored with PLS 6. They use the same synthetic observations and folds. The qualified build run shows lower OOF error for the two-source PLS 3 than the three-source PLS 3, but a still lower error when the full three-source model has six components. The qualified official build confirms these values in the actual native exports used by this support. The teaching observation is that adding sources can change the model capacity needed; it does not establish that MIR is a bad source. Compare OOF and keep the held-out test out of these adjustments.
slides.takeaway: Source contribution and model capacity must be considered together.

slides.title: Your next pipeline: use your sources, then make one edit
presenter_action: Import and map the real sources.
Start from a clear one-source or early pipeline.
Connect a purposeful measurement or change a model.
slides.speaker_notes: Show where the real Dataset Builder supplies the editor dataset, then return immediately to the pipeline. Invite each participant to name a source, its processing chain and the point where it should join. The full import details remain in the guide. End with two minutes of discussion about the concrete pipeline they will build, not a universal ranking of architectures.
slides.takeaway: Choose the source contribution first; make the pipeline express that decision.
